The resulting cyclo[n]carbon-based molecular junctions exhibit giant rectification ratios exceeding 103, while retaining exceptional structural robustness against variations in both donor chain length and carbon ring size. This work reveals the critical role of selective Fermi-level pinning in molecular junctions and provides a general design principle for engineering functional single-molecule electronic devices.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a molecular rectifier design using selective Fermi-level pinning to break transport symmetry, achieving giant rectification ratios (>10³) in cyclo[n]carbon-based junctions by suppressing occupied-state tunneling while favoring unoccupied molecular orbital transport.
AI.motivation: Achieving high rectification ratios in molecular-scale integrated circuits remains a long-standing challenge due to the intrinsic symmetry of resonant tunneling and the complexity of interfacial energy-level alignment.
AI.method: The authors propose a rectifier design strategy based on selective Fermi-level pinning, which breaks transport symmetry via pinning interactions between molecular frontier orbitals and electrodes, forcing tunneling to be predominantly governed by unoccupied molecular orbitals while suppressing occupied-state contributions.
AI.result: The cyclo[n]carbon-based molecular junctions exhibit giant rectification ratios exceeding 10³, with exceptional structural robustness against variations in donor chain length and carbon ring size.
AI.conclusion: Selective Fermi-level pinning is a critical mechanism in molecular junctions, and this work provides a general design principle for engineering functional single-molecule electronic devices.

title: Order-Disorder Tricriticality in $\mathrm{A}_n \mathrm{B}_n$ Star Polymer Melts
summary: Tricriticality usually requires tuning an additional thermodynamic parameter. Here we show that, in symmetric $\mathrm{A}_n\mathrm{B}_n$ star-polymer melts, the arm number $n$ itself plays this role and drives the order--disorder transition (ODT) from second order to first order. By developing a sixth-order free-energy expansion within the random phase approximation and comparing it with self-consistent field theory (SCFT) calculations, we analytically identify a tricritical arm number, $n_{\mathrm{tc}}\approx 5.4475$. For $n<n_{\mathrm{tc}}$, the lamellar ordering transition remains continuous and occurs at the spinodal point, $(χN)_{\mathrm{s}}\approx 10.495$. For $n>n_{\mathrm{tc}}$, the transition becomes first order, and $(χN)_{\mathrm{ODT}}$ shifts below $(χN)_{\mathrm{s}}$ with a quadratic dependence near the tricritical point. SCFT calculations confirm the predicted transition character and phase-boundary shift. The origin of this behavior is traced to inter-arm correlations generated by the common junction. We further show that the noninteger tricritical arm number can be effectively realized in binary mixtures of star polymers. This provides a rare analytically tractable example of architecture-induced tricriticality in a microphase-separating polymer system.

AI.tldr: In symmetric AₙBₙ star-polymer melts, the arm number n acts as a tuning parameter that drives the order-disorder transition from second-order to first-order, with a tricritical arm number n_tc ≈ 5.4475 identified analytically.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that arm number n in star-polymer melts can serve as a thermodynamic tuning parameter to control the order of the order-disorder transition, providing an analytically tractable example of architecture-induced tricriticality.
AI.method: A sixth-order free-energy expansion within the random phase approximation (RPA) was developed and compared with self-consistent field theory (SCFT) calculations. Binary mixtures of star polymers were also considered to realize noninteger tricritical arm numbers.
AI.result: A tricritical arm number n_tc ≈ 5.4475 was identified. For n < n_tc, the lamellar ordering transition is continuous at spinodal (χN)_s ≈ 10.495; for n > n_tc, the transition becomes first-order with (χN)_ODT shifting below (χN)_s. SCFT confirmed predicted behavior and phase-boundary shift.
AI.conclusion: Inter-arm correlations at the common junction drive this architecture-induced tricriticality. Noninteger tricritical arm numbers can be realized in binary star-polymer mixtures, offering a rare analytically tractable example in microphase-separating polymer systems.

title: Interaction-Split Edge Spectral Flow and Neutral Triplet Boundary Modes in a C = 2 Hubbard Pump
comment: 7 pages, 4 figures, plus Supplemental Material (4 pages, 6 figures)
summary: We show that a sliding spatial modulation of the on-site Hubbard interaction realizes a many-body Thouless pump whose boundary spectral flow is reconstructed by correlations. For a period-three Hubbard chain at filling $ρ=2/3$, density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) calculations identify a correlated insulator with many-body Chern number $C=+2$, corresponding to two units of charge pumped per cycle. Its excitation spectrum separates the charge gap from the lowest neutral spin gap, revealing an interacting bulk response beyond a simple spin-degenerate band pump. Under open boundary conditions, this contrast becomes even more pronounced. A spin-degenerate Hartree/Aubry-André-Harper reference pump exhibits simultaneous edge flow in the two spin channels, whereas the full modulated Hubbard model suppresses the boundary doublon channel and splits the spectral flow into two distinct edge events. Between these events, the boundary charge is neutralized while a neutral, spinful triplet-like excitation is localized at the edge. The global $μ-U$ phase diagram reveals filling-dependent topology: the $ρ=2/3$ regime remains in the $C=+2$ sector, while $ρ=4/3$ regime undergoes a spin-gap-closing transition from a $C=-2$ pump to a distinct $C=+1$ topological Mott pump.

AI.tldr: Sliding spatial modulation of Hubbard interaction realizes many-body Thouless pump with correlated edge spectral flow; at ρ=2/3, a C=+2 correlated insulator is identified, while ρ=4/3 shows a spin-gap-closing transition from C=-2 to C=+1 topological Mott pump.
AI.motivation: To understand how correlations reconstruct the boundary spectral flow of a Thouless pump beyond non-interacting or spin-degenerate approximations, and to map out the filling-dependent topological phase diagram of a modulated Hubbard chain.
AI.method: Density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) calculations on a period-three Hubbard chain at filling ρ=2/3 and ρ=4/3, computing many-body Chern numbers, charge and spin gaps, and edge spectral flow under open boundary conditions, with comparison to a Hartree/Aubry-André-Harper reference pump.
AI.result: A C=+2 correlated insulator with separated charge and spin gaps is found at ρ=2/3. Under open boundaries, the modulated Hubbard model suppresses doublon edge flow and splits spectral flow into two distinct events, with a neutral spinful triplet-like edge excitation between them. At ρ=4/3, a spin-gap-closing transition occurs from C=-2 to C=+1 topological Mott pump.
AI.conclusion: Correlation fundamentally alters the boundary physics of topological pumps, producing neutral edge excitations and filling-dependent transitions that are absent in non-interacting descriptions.

title: Pulsed thermal annealing enables switching of chiral antiferromagnetic order with a sub-millitesla field in Mn$_3$Sn
summary: The manipulation of antiferromagnetic (AFM) order is a central theme in modern spintronics. In this work, we achieve reliable switching of the chiral AFM state in the Weyl antiferromagnet Mn$_3$Sn using a heat pulse combined with a very small magnetic field as small as 0.1 mT. By systematically measuring the anomalous Hall effect (AHE) in high-quality single crystals, we show that the field needed for switching decreases as the temperature approaches the Néel temperature $T_N$, and vanishes at $T_N$. Pulsed thermal annealing above $T_N$ followed by cooling in a tiny external field enables full and reproducible switching of the magnetic octupole order. Our results show that thermal softening (heating above $T_N$ to temporarily remove the magnetic anisotropy) is a key step that lowers the energy barrier to nearly zero. This allows an extremely weak directional field (like the effective field from spin-orbit torque in thin-film devices) to set the final magnetic state during cooling. We also provide a simple model to estimate the temperature rise in nanoscale devices under current pulses, giving practical guidance for device design. This work highlights that thermal effects are not a side issue but an important partner to spin torques, and suggests that future work should take both into account.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates reliable switching of chiral AFM order in Mn₃Sn using a heat pulse combined with a tiny magnetic field (as low as 0.1 mT). Thermal annealing above the Néel temperature removes magnetic anisotropy, allowing a weak directional field to set the final state during cooling. This highlights thermal effects as essential, not incidental, to spintronic switching.
AI.motivation: To achieve reliable switching of antiferromagnetic order in the Weyl antiferromagnet Mn₃Sn using minimal magnetic fields, and to clarify the role of thermal effects in enabling such switching.
AI.method: Systematic measurement of the anomalous Hall effect (AHE) in high-quality single crystals of Mn₃Sn; pulsed thermal annealing above the Néel temperature combined with a small external magnetic field; modeling of temperature rise in nanoscale devices under current pulses.
AI.result: The required switching field decreases as temperature approaches TN and vanishes at TN. Full and reproducible switching of magnetic octupole order is achieved using thermal pulses above TN with fields as low as 0.1 mT. Thermal softening temporarily removes magnetic anisotropy, lowering the energy barrier to nearly zero.
AI.conclusion: Thermal effects are not a side issue but an important partner to spin torques in spintronic switching. Future work should consider both thermal and spin-torque effects together for device design.

title: Localized Excitonic Emission in Wafer-Scale MOCVD-Grown GaSe 2D Nanosheets for Classical and Non-Classical Light Sources
summary: Wafer-scale growth of two-dimensional semiconductors remains a key challenge for their integration into photonic technologies. While most studies of two-dimensional semiconductors have focused on transition metal dichalcogenides and their scalable fabrication, comparatively little attention has been given to III-VI monochalcogenides. Here, we report wafer-scale growth of gallium selenide (GaSe) by metal-organic chemical vapor deposition (MOCVD) and investigate its structural and optical properties for visible-range classical and quantum light emission. Two samples with thicknesses ranging from a few monolayers to several micrometers, controlled via the growth time, were investigated. The 30-minute grown sample yields intense, broad photoluminescence spanning 1.7--2.0$\,$eV, whereas the thinner 3-minute sample exhibits discrete narrow emission lines and single-photon emission with $(g^{(2)}(0) = 0.15 \pm 0.10)$. Remarkably, cathodoluminescence mapping reveals pronounced spatial localization of both spectrally narrow and broad emission centers. Together with temperature-dependent power-law analysis and Raman mapping, our results indicate defect-induced emission rather than intrinsic excitonic recombination. These findings establish wafer-scale MOCVD grown 2D GaSe as a platform for classical and non-classical light sources and highlight defect-engineered localization as a route toward scalable quantum photonics.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates wafer-scale growth of 2D gallium selenide (GaSe) via MOCVD, showing thickness-dependent optical properties: thick samples yield broad photoluminescence (1.7-2.0 eV) for classical light, while thin samples exhibit narrow emission lines and single-photon emission (g²(0)=0.15±0.10) for quantum light. Emission is attributed to defect-induced localization rather than intrinsic excitonic recombination, establishing GaSe as a scalable platform for classical and quantum photonics.
AI.motivation: Wafer-scale growth of two-dimensional semiconductors remains a key challenge for integrating them into photonic technologies, with III-VI monochalcogenides like GaSe receiving comparatively little attention despite their potential.
AI.method: GaSe was grown via metal-organic chemical vapor deposition (MOCVD) at wafer scale with two growth times (3 min and 30 min) to control thickness. Structural and optical properties were characterized using photoluminescence, cathodoluminescence mapping, Raman mapping, and temperature-dependent power-law analysis.
AI.result: The 30-min sample yields intense, broad photoluminescence (1.7-2.0 eV) for classical light; the 3-min sample exhibits discrete narrow emission lines and single-photon emission with g²(0)=0.15±0.10. Cathodoluminescence mapping reveals pronounced spatial localization of emission centers. Emission is defect-induced rather than intrinsic excitonic recombination.
AI.conclusion: Wafer-scale MOCVD-grown 2D GaSe is established as a platform for classical and non-classical light sources, with defect-engineered localization offering a route toward scalable quantum photonics.

title: Multi-field Return Point Memory
summary: Non-equilibrium systems display memory, a dependence not merely on their present environment but on previously applied fields. Multistable systems such as spin glasses, martensites and granular matter have exponentially many microstates consistent with an applied field, making their rich dynamics difficult to control. Control and order can be achieved through the concept of partial ordering, which we here generalize to systems subject to multiple control fields. We demonstrate, within the model system of the zero-temperature Ising model, that this leads to return-point memory, in which an applied sequence of fields restores the hysteretic system not only to a previous magnetization, but to a previous exact microstate. The multiplicity of fields grants more precise and complex control of the system, with different classes of operations displaying commutative and noncommutative behavior. This grants new insight into how physical systems can remember, learn, and be trained.

AI.tldr: The paper generalizes partial ordering to multistable non-equilibrium systems under multiple control fields, demonstrating return-point memory in the zero-temperature Ising model, where applied field sequences restore exact microstates, enabling more precise control with commutative/noncommutative operations.
AI.motivation: Non-equilibrium systems with multistability (spin glasses, martensites, granular matter) have exponentially many microstates, making their dynamics difficult to control. The authors seek to generalize partial ordering to achieve control and order in systems subject to multiple control fields.
AI.method: The study generalizes the concept of partial ordering to systems under multiple control fields and demonstrates it within the model system of the zero-temperature Ising model.
AI.result: This leads to return-point memory, where an applied sequence of fields restores the hysteretic system not only to a previous magnetization but to a previous exact microstate. The multiplicity of fields enables more precise and complex control, with different operations exhibiting both commutative and noncommutative behavior.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide new insight into how physical systems can remember, learn, and be trained through multiple control fields.

title: Non-adiabatic phonon renormalization in metallic versus insulating rutile oxides
comment: Accepted in Phys. Rev. B as a regular article (https://doi.org/10.1103/4nhr-dvbn)
summary: We present a comparative Raman scattering study of metallic rutile oxides (RuO$_2$ and IrO$_2$) and insulating rutiles (TiO$_2$ and SnO$_2$). Temperature-dependent Raman spectra reveal that the metallic compounds exhibit pronounced phonon frequency hardening, $ω(11~\mathrm{K})-ω(300~\mathrm{K})=Δω\approx 6$-$10~\mathrm{cm}^{-1}$, whereas the insulating rutiles show only modest hardening, $Δω\approx 1$-$3~\mathrm{cm}^{-1}$. In contrast, the linewidth changes, $ΔΓ\approx 1$--$7~\mathrm{cm}^{-1}$, do not display a systematic metallic-insulating classification. Fits with the conventional Klemens anharmonic decay model reproduce the overall temperature trends but yield inconsistent anharmonic parameters for the metallic compounds when benchmarked against insulating rutile analogues. A modified Klemens framework, incorporating an additional $T^{2}$ correction to the phonon frequency arising from the electronic contribution to the phonon self-energy, quantitatively accounts for the enhanced renormalization observed in metallic systems. These results establish finite non-adiabatic electron-phonon coupling in metallic rutiles and demonstrate that phonon renormalization can be identified even in the absence of observable Fano asymmetry in the phonon line shapes.

AI.tldr: Comparative Raman study of metallic (RuO₂, IrO₂) vs. insulating (TiO₂, SnO₂) rutiles reveals that metallic compounds exhibit pronounced phonon frequency hardening (Δω ≈ 6–10 cm⁻¹) versus modest hardening in insulators (Δω ≈ 1–3 cm⁻¹), explained by a modified Klemens model with an additional T² electronic term, establishing finite non-adiabatic electron-phonon coupling in metallic rutiles even without observable Fano asymmetry.
AI.motivation: To understand the role of electron-phonon coupling in metallic vs. insulating rutile oxides and to determine whether phonon renormalization signatures can be detected in metals even in the absence of Fano line shape asymmetry.
AI.method: Comparative temperature-dependent Raman scattering on metallic (RuO₂, IrO₂) and insulating (TiO₂, SnO₂) rutiles; analysis using the conventional Klemens anharmonic decay model and a modified version incorporating a T² electronic correction to the phonon self-energy.
AI.result: Metallic rutiles show pronounced phonon hardening (Δω ≈ 6–10 cm⁻¹), while insulators show modest hardening (Δω ≈ 1–3 cm⁻¹). Linewidth changes (ΔΓ ≈ 1–7 cm⁻¹) show no systematic metal-insulator distinction. The conventional Klemens model fits the trends but yields inconsistent anharmonic parameters for metals, whereas the modified model with a T² electronic term quantitatively captures the enhanced renormalization.
AI.conclusion: Finite non-adiabatic electron-phonon coupling exists in metallic rutiles, and phonon renormalization can identify electron-phonon interactions even when Fano asymmetry is absent.

title: Generalized Shift Vector as the Intrinsic Dipole of Many-Body Correlated Electronic States
summary: Shift vectors play a central role in nonlinear optics and transport phenomena, where they are usually understood as charge-center shifts associated with transitions between quantum states. Here we show that the same geometric structure can be more fundamentally understood as the intrinsic dipole moment of a single correlated state. Our derivation clarifies the local and global aspects of gauge invariance, the origin of the phase-gradient term, and its connection to the internal coherence structure of many-body correlations. The single-state shift character appears both as a displacement of the real-space joint probability density and as a linear electric-field modification in energy space. Applying this framework to optically induced correlations, electron-phonon-mediated processes, and excitonic electron-hole states, we recover previously proposed shift vectors and the standard expression for the shift current as special cases. Our results establish a common physical foundation for shift vectors as intrinsic dipolar properties of correlated electronic states.

AI.tldr: Shift vectors are redefined as intrinsic dipole moments of single correlated states, unifying nonlinear optics and transport phenomena under a common geometric foundation.
AI.motivation: To provide a more fundamental understanding of shift vectors beyond the conventional interpretation as charge-center shifts between transition states, and to establish their origin as intrinsic dipolar properties of individual correlated many-body states.
AI.method: The authors derive shift vectors from the intrinsic dipole moment of a single correlated state, analyzing gauge invariance, phase-gradient terms, and internal coherence of many-body correlations. They apply the framework to optically induced correlations, electron-phonon processes, and excitonic states.
AI.result: Shift vectors appear as both real-space joint probability density displacements and linear electric-field modifications in energy space. Known shift vectors and the standard shift current expression are recovered as special cases.
AI.conclusion: Shift vectors are fundamentally intrinsic dipolar properties of correlated electronic states, providing a unified physical foundation for phenomena in nonlinear optics and transport.

title: Orientable Surfactants on Thin Liquid Films: A Dynamic Density-Functional Theory Approach
summary: Thin liquid films are ubiquitous across many natural and engineering systems, including films which are laden with surface active molecules, i.e. surfactants. The presence of surfactants may have a destabilising effect on the film owing to their influence on surface tension, the so-called Marangoni effect, which in turn can induce flows in the film. Classical thin-film models for surfactant-laden films lead to paradigmatic gradient dynamics equations governing the film height and surfactant concentration and have been widely studied. However, in all these works, which are based on fluid dynamics or nonequilibrium thermodynamics, the shape of surfactants is neglected, and they have been treated as symmetric point-like particles. In general, this is a drastic oversimplification, as surfactants are amphiphilic with a polar head-tail structure. To account for this effect we use elements from the statistical mechanics of classical fluids, namely density-functional theory (DFT), and its dynamic extension (DDFT). Starting from DDFT and under the long-wave approximation, we derive the pertinent thin-film equations with the surfactants treated as polar uniaxial particles. These are equations which govern the film height, as well as the surfactant concentration and polarisation field. They preserve the gradient dynamics form by appropriately defining the free energy, which contains the usual interfacial contributions, as well as further contributions from the polarisation field. In doing so, we uncover a novel form of a generalised surface tension that is dependent on the surfactant polarisation as well as concentration, and show that it arises in a thermodynamically consistent way.

AI.tldr: The paper derives thin-film equations for surfactant-laden films using density-functional theory, treating surfactants as polar uniaxial particles with a head-tail structure. This yields a generalized surface tension dependent on both surfactant concentration and polarization, preserving gradient dynamics form.
AI.motivation: Classical thin-film models treat surfactants as symmetric point-like particles, neglecting their amphiphilic head-tail structure. This oversimplification limits understanding of surfactant-induced Marangoni effects on film stability.
AI.method: Starting from dynamic density-functional theory (DDFT) and applying the long-wave approximation, the authors derive thin-film equations treating surfactants as polar uniaxial particles, defining a free energy that includes interfacial and polarization contributions.
AI.result: The derived equations govern film height, surfactant concentration, and polarization field, preserving gradient dynamics. A novel generalized surface tension emerges that depends on both surfactant concentration and polarization, derived in a thermodynamically consistent manner.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating surfactant shape (polar head-tail structure) via DFT/DDFT reveals new physics in thin-film dynamics, specifically a polarization-dependent surface tension, which classical point-like surfactant models cannot capture.

title: Thermodynamic stability of twisted domains in AgCrSe$_{2}$ thin films grown on lattice-matched YSZ(111) substrate
summary: Control of structural domains in epitaxial thin films of functional materials is a fundamental technique to utilize their intrinsic physical and chemical properties in solid-state devices. In this study, we report on suppression of twisted-domain formation in thin-film growth of polar magnetic semiconductor AgCrSe$_{2}$ using pulsed-laser deposition. In exploring concomitant optimized growth temperature and Ag/Cr composition ratio of supply, we find the critical growth temperature ($T\mathrm{_{sub}}$) for obtaining single 60$^{\circ}$ domain in c-axis oriented AgCrSe$_{2}$ thin film on a lattice-matched (111) plane of the yttria-stabilized zirconia substrate. At temperatures below and above the critical $T\mathrm{_{sub}}$, metastable 0$^{\circ}$ domain in addition to the 60$^{\circ}$ domain emerges, indicating delicate energy balance of thermodynamic stability for obtaining the single-domain structure. Surface structural analysis using time-of-flight low-energy atom scattering spectroscopy reveals the presence of two polar orientations along $+Z$ and $-Z$ directions. These findings provide valuable insights into the thin-film growth mechanisms for a family of two-dimensional compounds with rhombohedral lattices.

AI.tldr: The study demonstrates suppression of twisted-domain formation in epitaxial thin films of polar magnetic semiconductor AgCrSe₂ by optimizing growth temperature and composition ratio, achieving single 60° domain on YSZ(111) substrate, with evidence of two polar orientations.
AI.motivation: Controlling structural domains in epitaxial thin films of functional materials is essential for utilizing their intrinsic physical and chemical properties in solid-state devices.
AI.method: Pulsed-laser deposition (PLD) was used to grow AgCrSe₂ thin films on lattice-matched YSZ(111) substrates, with systematic exploration of growth temperature and Ag/Cr composition ratio. Surface structure was analyzed using time-of-flight low-energy atom scattering spectroscopy.
AI.result: A critical substrate temperature (T_sub) was identified for obtaining a single 60° domain in c-axis oriented AgCrSe₂ thin films. Below and above this critical temperature, a metastable 0° domain appears alongside the 60° domain. Two polar orientations along +Z and -Z directions were observed on the surface.
AI.conclusion: These findings provide valuable insights into thin-film growth mechanisms for a family of two-dimensional compounds with rhombohedral lattices, highlighting the delicate thermodynamic balance required for single-domain structure formation.

title: Graphene-based Photodetector with Engineered Hot Carrier Cooling Dynamics
summary: Graphene has emerged as a promising material for integration into silicon photonics, owing to its ultrafast and broadband photoresponse without the need for an external bias voltage. This photoresponse relies on the photo-thermoelectric effect created by hot carriers. A key factor underlying the performance of graphene photodetectors is the cooling dynamics of these hot carriers. In this work, we engineer these dynamics in a WSe2-graphene-WSe2 waveguide-integrated photodetector. In particular, by introducing proximity screening by a nearby graphite layer to this structure, we prolong the hot-carrier cooling time, leading to an enhanced photoresponse. We characterize the cooling dynamics under continuous-wave laser excitation by employing a photomixing technique, revealing an increase in the cooling time by up to a factor of four. Direct photoresponse measurements show that the internal photoresponsivity improves by approximately 50%. Together, these results demonstrate the potential of proximity screening to enhance the performance of graphene-based photodetectors on an integrated photonics platform.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that introducing proximity screening via a graphite layer in a WSe2-graphene-WSe2 waveguide-integrated photodetector prolongs hot-carrier cooling time by up to 4x and improves internal photoresponsivity by ~50%, enhancing graphene photodetector performance.
AI.motivation: Graphene's photoresponse relies on the photo-thermoelectric effect driven by hot carriers, and the cooling dynamics of these carriers is a key limiting factor for photodetector performance. Engineering these dynamics can enhance device performance.
AI.method: A WSe2-graphene-WSe2 waveguide-integrated photodetector was fabricated with a nearby graphite layer for proximity screening. Cooling dynamics were characterized under continuous-wave laser excitation using a photomixing technique.
AI.result: Proximity screening increased the hot-carrier cooling time by up to a factor of four, and the internal photoresponsivity improved by approximately 50%.
AI.conclusion: Proximity screening is an effective approach to enhance the performance of graphene-based photodetectors on an integrated photonics platform.

title: In situ estimation of local acoustic pressure amplitude by force balancing with a ferrofluid droplet probe
summary: Acoustic tweezers enable non-contact manipulation of microscale objects, but quantitative in situ evaluation of the peak local pressure amplitude remains difficult in confined devices. Conventional hydrophone-based measurements are often limited at the microscale by probe size and installation constraints. Here, we present a force-balance method in which a trapped ferrofluid droplet serves as a local probe in a standing-wave acoustic field and an externally applied magnetic-field gradient is tuned so that the magnetic force balances the maximum primary acoustic radiation force on the droplet. From the magnetic force on the ferrofluid droplet, determined at the balance point, we estimate a peak local pressure amplitude of $2.6\times10^{5}$~Pa for 7.2~MHz operation at 10~V$_{\mathrm{pp}}$. This approach provides a practical route for quantitative in situ characterization of microscale acoustic fields and for setting operating conditions in compact acoustofluidic devices.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a force-balance method using a trapped ferrofluid droplet as a local probe to measure peak local pressure amplitude in microscale acoustic fields, achieving an estimated pressure of 2.6×10⁵ Pa at 7.2 MHz operation.
AI.motivation: Quantitative in situ evaluation of peak local pressure amplitude remains difficult in confined microscale acoustofluidic devices because conventional hydrophone-based measurements are limited by probe size and installation constraints.
AI.method: A ferrofluid droplet is trapped in a standing-wave acoustic field, and an externally applied magnetic-field gradient is tuned to balance the magnetic force against the maximum primary acoustic radiation force on the droplet. The peak local pressure amplitude is then estimated from the magnetic force at the balance point.
AI.result: The method yields an estimated peak local pressure amplitude of 2.6×10⁵ Pa for 7.2 MHz operation at 10 Vpp.
AI.conclusion: This force-balance approach provides a practical route for quantitative in situ characterization of microscale acoustic fields and for setting operating conditions in compact acoustofluidic devices.

title: Commensuration torques in double-moiré twisted trilayer hexagonal boron nitride and graphene heterostructures
summary: We study commensuration-driven torques and angle locking in double-moiré trilayer hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) and graphene heterostructures using large-scale atomistic relaxations. In twisted trilayer hBN (t3BN) homostructures, double-moiré commensuration ($θ_{12} = -θ_{23}$) give rise to local energy minima accompanied by torque sign reversals, signaling a restoring tendency toward the commensurate configuration. The corresponding binding energies are $\sim$0.2-0.3 meV/atom, originating from enhanced overlap of low-energy stacking domains, although the system is globally stable at zero twist. In contrast, in graphene/hBN heterolayers systems the global energy minimum can coincide with the double-moiré commensuration angle, particularly near $\sim$0.6$^{\circ}$, reflecting competition between lattice mismatch and interfacial relaxation. Incommensurate atomic structures have reduced stabilization due to suppressed overlap of low-energy stacking and have enhanced superlubricity due to spatial averaging of interfacial energies. These results establish double-moiré commensuration as a general, system-dependent mechanism for twist-angle stabilization, whose angular stability is characterized by the torque magnitude and binding energy. Coulomb electrostatic interactions further enhance the stabilization energy without changing the underlying physics.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how double-moiré commensuration (matching twist angles between layers) generates torques and locks twist angles in trilayer hBN and graphene/hBN heterostructures. In t3BN, commensuration creates local energy minima with torque sign reversals (~0.2-0.3 meV/atom binding energy). In graphene/hBN, the global minimum can occur at commensuration angles (e.g., ~0.6°), while incommensurate structures reduce stability but enhance superlubricity.
AI.motivation: To understand the mechanism of twist-angle stabilization in double-moiré trilayer systems, specifically how commensuration between two moiré patterns generates torques and locking effects, and to compare this across homostructures (t3BN) and heterostructures (graphene/hBN).
AI.method: Large-scale atomistic relaxations were used to study commensuration-driven torques and angle locking in double-moiré trilayer hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) and graphene heterostructures.
AI.result: In t3BN, double-moiré commensuration (θ₁₂ = -θ₂₃) yields local energy minima with torque sign reversals and binding energies ~0.2-0.3 meV/atom. In graphene/hBN, the global minimum can coincide with double-moiré commensuration near ~0.6°. Incommensurate structures show reduced stability and enhanced superlubricity. Coulomb interactions enhance stabilization energy without altering underlying physics.
AI.conclusion: Double-moiré commensuration is a general but system-dependent mechanism for twist-angle stabilization, characterized by torque magnitude and binding energy.

title: Momentum-Resolved Tunneling Modulation Induced Giant Multistate Resistance in Antiferroelectric Multiferroic Junction
summary: Multiferroic tunnel junctions (MFTJs), integrating ferroelectric and ferromagnetic functionalities within a single nanoscale device, hold significant promise for non-volatile, multi-state memory and innovative computing paradigms. In conventional MFTJs, tunneling resistance modulation relies primarily on ferroelectric (FE) polarization switching, which alters interfacial electric fields and shifts the Fermi level of adjacent ferromagnetic electrodes. However, achieving high tunnelelectroresistance (TER) through this approach demands strong built-in electric fields, which simultaneously hinder FE polarization switching, creating an intrinsic trade-off between reliable data reading and efficient writing. Here, we propose a dual mechanism that combines antiferroelectric (AFE) phase-transition modulation of the evanescent decay states with interfacial spin filtering based on $Fe_3GaTe_2$/bilayer-$In_2Se_3$/$Fe_3GaTe_2$ heterostructure. Beyond altering the electrostatic potential as in AFE-FE switching, the transitions between head-type and tail-type AFE states preserve the centrosymmetric potential profile yet fundamentally modulate the momentum-resolved distribution of evanescent decay rates across the Brillouin zone. When integrated with perfect spin filtering at the $Fe_3GaTe_2$/$α$-$In_2Se_3$ interface, this mechanism yields a giant TER (~$7.6\times10^3\%$), over 4 times that of conventional FE-based MFTJs, and a TMR exceeding $6.8\times10^5\%$, enhanced by two orders of magnitude over typical MFTJs. These mechanisms resolve the performance trade-off in MFTJs, enabling six distinct non-volatile resistance states at room temperature.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a dual mechanism combining antiferroelectric phase-transition modulation and interfacial spin filtering in Fe₃GaTe₂/bilayer-In₂Se₃/Fe₃GaTe₂ heterostructures, achieving giant TER (~7.6×10³%) and TMR (>6.8×10⁵%) while resolving the intrinsic trade-off between reading and writing in conventional multiferroic tunnel junctions.
AI.motivation: Conventional MFTJs face an intrinsic trade-off between reliable data reading and efficient writing: achieving high tunnel electroresistance (TER) requires strong built-in electric fields, but these fields simultaneously hinder ferroelectric polarization switching.
AI.method: A dual mechanism combining (1) antiferroelectric (AFE) phase-transition modulation of evanescent decay states and (2) interfacial spin filtering, realized in a Fe₃GaTe₂/bilayer-In₂Se₃/Fe₃GaTe₂ heterostructure. The head-type/tail-type AFE state transitions preserve centrosymmetric potential but modulate momentum-resolved evanescent decay rates across the Brillouin zone.
AI.result: Giant TER of ~7.6×10³% (over 4× that of conventional FE-based MFTJs) and TMR exceeding 6.8×10⁵% (enhanced by two orders of magnitude). Six distinct non-volatile resistance states at room temperature.
AI.conclusion: The proposed mechanism resolves the performance trade-off in MFTJs, enabling multi-state non-volatile memory with simultaneously enhanced reading and writing capabilities at room temperature.

title: Studying Creep-Fatigue interaction of Nickel-Based Superalloys using Crystal Plasticity and Entropy-Based life prediction model
summary: Creep-fatigue interaction in single-crystal nickel superalloys is difficult to predict because the response depends on the combined effects of loading parameters, hold time, temperature, and the underlying deformation mechanisms. This is important for turbine blade applications, where components experience both fatigue and creep during service. In the present work, a crystal plasticity finite element (CPFE) framework is used to study the creep-fatigue response of a single-crystal nickel superalloy under a range of practically relevant thermo-mechanical loading conditions. In particular, the effects of strain amplitude, R-ratio, hold duration, and temperature on cyclic deformation, stress relaxation, damage evolution, and creep-fatigue life are examined. Particular attention is given to separate the roles of fatigue and creep damage, understanding their interaction, and identify the creep-dominated and fatigue-dominated regimes as a function of strain amplitude and hold time. The study brings together these effects within a single framework and shows that the predicted trends in cyclic response and life are in good agreement with experimental observations reported in the literature.

AI.tldr: The paper uses a crystal plasticity finite element (CPFE) framework to study creep-fatigue interaction in single-crystal nickel superalloys, examining effects of strain amplitude, R-ratio, hold duration, and temperature on cyclic deformation, stress relaxation, damage evolution, and life. It identifies creep-dominated and fatigue-dominated regimes and validates predictions against experimental observations.
AI.motivation: Creep-fatigue interaction in single-crystal nickel superalloys is difficult to predict due to combined effects of loading parameters, hold time, temperature, and deformation mechanisms, yet it is critical for turbine blade applications where components experience both fatigue and creep during service.
AI.method: A crystal plasticity finite element (CPFE) framework is used to model the creep-fatigue response under a range of thermo-mechanical loading conditions. The study systematically examines strain amplitude, R-ratio, hold duration, and temperature effects on cyclic deformation, stress relaxation, damage evolution, and life.
AI.result: The framework successfully separates the roles of fatigue and creep damage, identifies creep-dominated and fatigue-dominated regimes as functions of strain amplitude and hold time, and produces predicted trends in cyclic response and life that agree well with experimental observations from the literature.
AI.conclusion: The CPFE framework provides a unified approach to predict creep-fatigue interaction in single-crystal nickel superalloys under practically relevant thermo-mechanical loading conditions, with validated accuracy against experimental data.

title: Nonreciprocal conductance in uniformly dissipative devices
summary: When studying non-Hermitian electronic systems, an obvious question is how various non-Hermitian effects affect measurable quantities like the conductance. Here, we show that uniformly dissipative circuits can exhibit nonreciprocal conductance, meaning that the two nonlocal conductances are different. We describe how this happens through a difference in transmission times between left-moving and right-moving electrons. We consider a specific case of a dissipative Rashba nanowire with a skewed magnetic field, and show how this difference in transmission times comes about through interference inside the circuit, and how this is modified as the dissipation strength changes.

AI.tldr: Uniformly dissipative circuits can exhibit nonreciprocal conductance—where two nonlocal conductances differ—due to a difference in transmission times between left- and right-moving electrons, as demonstrated in a dissipative Rashba nanowire with a skewed magnetic field where interference effects modify the conductance asymmetry with changing dissipation strength.
AI.motivation: To understand how non-Hermitian effects in dissipative electronic systems influence measurable quantities like conductance, specifically exploring whether uniformly dissipative circuits can break conductance reciprocity.
AI.method: The authors analyze nonreciprocal conductance theoretically in uniformly dissipative circuits by examining transmission time asymmetries between left- and right-moving electrons, using a dissipative Rashba nanowire with a skewed magnetic field as a concrete model system to study interference effects as a function of dissipation strength.
AI.result: Uniformly dissipative circuits can indeed exhibit nonreciprocal conductance, arising from unequal transmission times for electrons moving in opposite directions, with the asymmetry tunable by dissipation strength through interference effects in the circuit.
AI.conclusion: Dissipation alone, even when uniformly distributed, can break conductance reciprocity in electronic systems, offering a mechanism to engineer nonreciprocal transport via controlled dissipation in quantum devices.

title: A Metadynamics-Based Framework for Free Energy Surface Mapping of Multiparticle Diffusion in Crystals
summary: We propose two metadynamics (MetaD)-based methodologies for efficiently mapping free energy surfaces (FESs) of multiple interacting carriers diffusing in crystalline solids. Our approaches circumvent the challenges of high-dimensional collective variables (CVs) by employing replica state exchange MetaD and parallel bias MetaD, both of which decompose the high-dimensional CVs into multiple lower-dimensional ones. As a benchmark, we investigate two-dimensional lithium (Li) diffusion in LixTiS2 across a wide range of Li concentrations. The Li jump frequencies estimated from the obtained FESs exhibit concentration- and temperature-dependent trends consistent with previous kinetic Monte Carlo simulations and nuclear magnetic resonance measurements. Our approaches provide a promising framework for capturing the slow dynamics of diffusive carriers that are typically inaccessible to conventional molecular dynamics simulations.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes two metadynamics-based methods (replica state exchange MetaD and parallel bias MetaD) that decompose high-dimensional collective variables into lower-dimensional ones to map free energy surfaces of multiple interacting carriers diffusing in crystalline solids, demonstrated on Li diffusion in LixTiS2.
AI.motivation: To circumvent the challenges posed by high-dimensional collective variables when mapping free energy surfaces of multiple interacting diffusing carriers in crystalline solids, which are typically inaccessible to conventional molecular dynamics simulations.
AI.method: Two metadynamics-based methodologies: (1) replica state exchange MetaD and (2) parallel bias MetaD, both decomposing high-dimensional collective variables into multiple lower-dimensional ones.
AI.result: Li jump frequencies estimated from the obtained FESs show concentration- and temperature-dependent trends consistent with previous kinetic Monte Carlo simulations and NMR measurements.
AI.conclusion: The approaches provide a promising framework for capturing slow dynamics of diffusive carriers that are typically inaccessible to conventional molecular dynamics simulations.

title: Orbital Selective Dirac-like States in EuAgAs Revealed by Polarization Dependent ARPES and DFT
summary: Magnetic topological semimetals provide a promising platform for emergent quantum phenomena driven by the interplay between magnetism and relativistic fermions, including anomalous transport effects and tunable topological phases. Here, we investigate the electronic structure and orbital character of EuAgAs, a magnetic topological Dirac semimetal candidate, using density functional theory (DFT) and polarization dependent angle resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES). Fermi surface mapping and constant energy contours measured at 9 eV reveal ring like features that systematically expand with increasing binding energy, consistent with nearly linear low energy Dirac like dispersion. ARPES measurements at different photon energies hint at the presence of a van Hove singularity predicted by DFT calculations. Furthermore, this indicates that the photoemission matrix elements are highly sensitive to the excitation energy, allowing different photon energies to selectively probe distinct orbital characters. Polarization dependent ARPES measurements performed in s- and p-polarized geometries exhibit pronounced variations in spectral intensity, indicating symmetry selective orbital contributions to electronic states. These matrix element driven intensity modulations are well reproduced by DFT calculations. Furthermore, the observed Dirac like states remain nearly unchanged over the temperature range from 9 K to 30 K, suggesting that the magnetic ordering has minimal influence on the electronic structure. Our combined experimental and theoretical results provide detailed insight into the orbital selective electronic structure of EuAgAs and its implications for magnetic topological quantum states.

AI.tldr: This paper combines DFT and ARPES to investigate the electronic structure and orbital character of EuAgAs, a magnetic topological Dirac semimetal candidate, revealing Dirac-like dispersion, a van Hove singularity, symmetry-selective orbital contributions, and minimal influence of magnetic ordering on electronic states.
AI.motivation: To understand the interplay between magnetism and relativistic fermions in magnetic topological semimetals, specifically by investigating the electronic structure and orbital character of EuAgAs.
AI.method: Density functional theory (DFT) calculations combined with polarization-dependent angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES), including Fermi surface mapping, photon-energy-dependent measurements, and s-/p-polarized geometry measurements.
AI.result: Ring-like Fermi surface features with linear Dirac-like dispersion; van Hove singularity hinted at by ARPES and predicted by DFT; strong sensitivity of photoemission matrix elements to excitation energy and polarization; Dirac-like states remain nearly unchanged from 9 K to 30 K.
AI.conclusion: The combined experimental and theoretical results provide detailed insight into the orbital-selective electronic structure of EuAgAs and its implications for magnetic topological quantum states, suggesting minimal influence of magnetic ordering on the electronic structure.

title: Symmetry-protected nodal planes and accidental nodal surfaces in mixed odd-even wave spin-momentum locking of relativistic altermagnets
summary: Non-relativistic spin--momentum locking in altermagnets exhibits an even number of nodal planes. In the relativistic limit, the number of nodal planes can be lowered by symmetry reduction due to the Néel vector and spin--orbit coupling in noncentrosymmetric systems. Therefore, an analysis of the evolution of the nodal planes in relativistic altermagnets is required. While $g$-wave spin--momentum locking is straightforward to realize in non-relativistic altermagnets, this $g$-wave does not necessarily survive in the relativistic case. In this work, we investigate the relativistic spin--momentum locking of the centrosymmetric CrSb and the noncentrosymmetric wurtzite MnTe. As a first result, we show that in both systems the dominant spin component retains its $g$-wave character in the relativistic regime only when the Néel vector is oriented along the $z$-axis, while the subdominant components exhibit $d$-wave symmetry in CrSb and $p$-wave symmetry in ferroelectric wurtzite MnTe. More generally, the $g$-wave character is preserved in the relativistic limit only when both the Néel vector and the electric field associated with inversion-symmetry breaking are oriented along the $z$-axis. As a second result, we show that relativistic spin--momentum locking of ferroelectric altermagnets can exhibit $p$-wave magnetism with one symmetry-protected nodal plane and an accidental nodal surface not protected by symmetry, or can have two accidental nodal surfaces. With the Néel vector aligned along the $x$-axis, selected bands of ferroelectric altermagnet wurtzite MnTe exhibit $p$-wave magnetism. Our results establish that altermagnets can host distinct spin components that realize a mixture of angular-momentum wave symmetries in momentum space in the relativistic limit.

AI.tldr: This work analyzes relativistic spin–momentum locking in altermagnets (centrosymmetric CrSb and noncentrosymmetric wurtzite MnTe), showing that the dominant $g$-wave character is preserved only when the Néel vector and (if present) the electric field align along the $z$-axis, while subdominant components exhibit $d$- or $p$-wave symmetries; ferroelectric altermagnets can host $p$-wave magnetism with nodal surfaces.
AI.motivation: Non-relativistic altermagnets feature an even number of nodal planes, but relativistic effects (Néel vector orientation and spin–orbit coupling in noncentrosymmetric systems) can reduce the number of nodal planes. Thus, a systematic analysis of how nodal planes and spin–momentum locking evolve from the non-relativistic to the relativistic regime is needed.
AI.method: The authors investigate relativistic spin–momentum locking in two altermagnetic systems: centrosymmetric CrSb and noncentrosymmetric wurtzite MnTe. They analyze the symmetry and wave character of spin components under different Néel vector orientations and, for MnTe, the combined influence of inversion-symmetry breaking (ferroelectricity).
AI.result: (1) The dominant spin component retains $g$-wave character in the relativistic regime only when the Néel vector is along the $z$-axis; subdominant components show $d$-wave (CrSb) or $p$-wave (MnTe) symmetry. (2) $g$-wave is preserved only when both the Néel vector and the electric field (from inversion-symmetry breaking) are along $z$. (3) Ferroelectric altermagnets can exhibit $p$-wave magnetism with one symmetry-protected nodal plane and an accidental nodal surface, or two accidental nodal surfaces; with Néel vector along $x$, selected bands of MnTe realize $p$-wave magnetism.
AI.conclusion: Altermagnets can host distinct spin components with mixed angular-momentum wave symmetries (e.g., $g$, $d$, $p$) in momentum space under relativistic conditions, establishing a richer symmetry landscape than the non-relativistic picture suggests.

title: Self-organized formation of step-terrace structure in SrRuO3 thin films grown on mixed-terminated SrTiO3 (100) substrates
summary: Surface morphology of the substrate and bottom layers plays a critical role in the epitaxial growth of oxide thin films. Here, we report on the self-organized formation of a step-terrace structure in SrRuO3 (SRO) thin films grown using pulsed laser deposition on mixed-terminated SrTiO3 (100) substrates without any prior surface treatment. Atomic force microscopy observations reveal that SRO films initially grow in a three-dimensional island mode and subsequently undergo a transition to a step-flow growth mode through island coalescence as the film thickness increases, resulting in a well-defined step-terrace morphology with a step height consistent with the SRO unit-cell parameter. The average terrace width of the self-organized structure can be systematically tuned by varying the substrate temperature and the target-substrate distance, which we attribute to changes in the critical island radius that governs the nucleation behavior. To demonstrate the utility of this self-organized morphology, we show that BiFeO3 thin films grown on SRO films with such a step-terrace structure exhibit improved surface flatness and crystalline quality compared to those grown directly on bare SrTiO3 substrates. These findings provide a clear understanding of the mechanism of thickness-driven growth-mode transitions in perovskite oxide thin films under various growth conditions.

AI.tldr: SrRuO3 thin films on mixed-terminated SrTiO3 substrates self-organize into step-terrace structures via a transition from 3D island to step-flow growth mode, with tunable terrace width, and improve the quality of subsequently grown BiFeO3 films.
AI.motivation: To understand and exploit the self-organized formation of step-terrace structures in oxide thin films without prior substrate surface treatment, enabling improved epitaxial growth of functional oxide heterostructures.
AI.method: Pulsed laser deposition of SrRuO3 on mixed-terminated SrTiO3(100); atomic force microscopy to monitor growth mode transition; systematic variation of substrate temperature and target-substrate distance to tune terrace width; demonstration using BiFeO3 overgrowth.
AI.result: SRO films transition from 3D island to step-flow growth upon thickness increase, forming self-organized step-terraces with unit-cell step height; terrace width is tunable via growth parameters; BFO films on such SRO templates show improved flatness and crystallinity.
AI.conclusion: The self-organized step-terrace morphology arises from thickness-driven growth-mode transition governed by critical island radius, offering a simple route to obtain high-quality oxide thin film templates without substrate pretreatment.

title: Nonequilibrium dynamics of high energy transitions in monolayer WSe$_{2}$
summary: High-energy optical transitions in monolayer transition-metal dichalcogenides exhibit characteristics that are markedly distinct from those of lower-lying band-edge excitons. These differences arise from the involvement of electronic states located at regions of the Brillouin zone that are displaced from the $K$ valleys. In this work, we investigate the ultrafast dynamics of these high-energy excitations by employing broadband ultrafast transient absorption spectroscopy spanning the visible to ultraviolet spectral range. We observe that the formation and relaxation dynamics of one of the high energy transitions display a distinct behavior compared to the lower-energy excitonic resonances, developing on a significantly slower timescale. First-principles calculations of the excitonic landscape allow us to account for this delayed response and attribute it to the phonon-mediated formation of momentum-dark excitons.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the ultrafast dynamics of high-energy optical transitions in monolayer transition-metal dichalcogenides using broadband transient absorption spectroscopy, finding that high-energy excitons form and relax more slowly than band-edge excitons due to phonon-mediated formation of momentum-dark excitons, as supported by first-principles calculations.
AI.motivation: To understand the distinct ultrafast dynamics of high-energy optical transitions in monolayer TMDs, which involve electronic states away from the K valleys, and to explain their slower formation and relaxation compared to band-edge excitons.
AI.method: Broadband ultrafast transient absorption spectroscopy spanning visible to ultraviolet range, combined with first-principles calculations of the excitonic landscape.
AI.result: High-energy transitions exhibit significantly slower formation and relaxation dynamics compared to lower-energy excitonic resonances.
AI.conclusion: The delayed response of high-energy transitions is attributed to phonon-mediated formation of momentum-dark excitons, as revealed by first-principles calculations.

title: Ambiguity in B-Site cation ordering: A Case study of the double perovskite Ca$_2$CoNbO$_6$
summary: The ordering of cations in the B sublattice remains a challenging issue in double perovskites. In this work, a combined experimental and theoretical approach was employed to investigate the Co/Nb distribution in Ca$_2$CoNbO$_6$ and its influence on magnetic and transport properties. The density functional theory, supported by magnetic susceptibility measurements, indicates that Co adopts a high-spin Co$^{3+}$ state. No long-range magnetic ordering was observed down to low temperatures; however, the presence of short-range correlations points to the partial disorder in the Co/Nb sublattice. This interpretation is further supported by electron paramagnetic resonance, which also reveals slight oxygen nonstoichiometry. Electrical transport follows a small-polaron hopping mechanism with an activation energy of 0.25 eV. The Seebeck coefficient reaches 0.4 mV/K at 600 K.

AI.tldr: This study investigates the Co/Nb cation ordering in Ca₂CoNbO₆ double perovskite using combined experimental (magnetic susceptibility, EPR, transport measurements) and theoretical (DFT) methods. Co exists as high-spin Co³⁺, with partial disorder in the B sublattice leading to short-range magnetic correlations rather than long-range order, and electrical transport occurs via small-polaron hopping with a Seebeck coefficient of 0.4 mV/K at 600 K.
AI.motivation: To resolve the challenging issue of cation ordering in the B sublattice of double perovskites by investigating the Co/Nb distribution in Ca₂CoNbO₆ and understanding its impact on magnetic and transport properties.
AI.method: Combined experimental and theoretical approach: density functional theory (DFT), magnetic susceptibility measurements, electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR), electrical transport and Seebeck coefficient measurements.
AI.result: Co exists as high-spin Co³⁺; no long-range magnetic ordering below low temperatures; short-range correlations indicate partial Co/Nb sublattice disorder; EPR reveals slight oxygen nonstoichiometry; electrical transport follows small-polaron hopping (Eₐ = 0.25 eV); Seebeck coefficient = 0.4 mV/K at 600 K.
AI.conclusion: Partial disorder in the Co/Nb sublattice governs the magnetic and transport behavior of Ca₂CoNbO₆, with high-spin Co³⁺, short-range magnetic correlations, and small-polaron hopping conduction.

title: First-principles transition-state tensorial cluster expansion of vacancy diffusion in Ta-W beyond the kinetically-resolved activation approximation
summary: Predicting diffusion in chemically complex alloys remains challenging due to the strong dependence of migration barriers on local atomic environments. Here, we develop a first-principles-informed framework that directly learns environment-dependent migration barriers without relying on reduced kinetic approximations such as the kinetically resolved activation (KRA) model. Migration barriers computed using density functional theory and nudged elastic band calculations are represented via a tensorial cluster expansion including transition states and deployed in on-lattice kinetic Monte Carlo simulations. Applied to the Ta-W system, the framework captures nontrivial composition-dependent diffusion behavior arising from a crossover between solute trapping and percolated low-barrier transport pathways, yielding a maximum in the apparent activation energy near intermediate compositions. This approach establishes a general and scalable route for integrating first-principles transition-state energetics into mesoscale kinetic simulations, enabling predictive multiscale modeling of diffusion in chemically complex materials and providing a pathway for uncovering emergent transport phenomena.

AI.tldr: A first-principles-informed framework learns environment-dependent migration barriers in chemically complex alloys using tensorial cluster expansion and on-lattice KMC, applied to Ta-W system to capture composition-dependent diffusion behavior with a maximum apparent activation energy at intermediate compositions.
AI.motivation: Predicting diffusion in chemically complex alloys is challenging due to the strong dependence of migration barriers on local atomic environments; existing reduced approximations (e.g., KRA model) are insufficient.
AI.method: Migration barriers from DFT+NEB are represented via a tensorial cluster expansion including transition states, deployed in on-lattice kinetic Monte Carlo simulations.
AI.result: The framework captures nontrivial composition-dependent diffusion from a crossover between solute trapping and percolated low-barrier transport pathways, yielding a maximum apparent activation energy near intermediate compositions.
AI.conclusion: This approach establishes a general, scalable route for integrating first-principles transition-state energetics into mesoscale kinetic simulations for predictive multiscale modeling of diffusion in chemically complex materials.

title: Close correlation between giant magnetostriction and the microstructure in Fe-Ga melt-spun ribbons
summary: Magnetoelastic anisotropy and <100> texture are crucial for promoting magnetostriction in Galfenol (Fe-Ga). Given that single-crystal Fe-Ga remains technically demanding and low magnetostriction of polycrystal, we explore melt-spun as an alternative, where rare-earth (RE) doping and cooling rates optimizing enable controllable <100> textured with required magnetoelastic anisotropy. Fe81Ga19 binary ribbons and RE-doped ribbons (0.2 at.% Pr, 1 at.% Pr and 1 at.% Ce) were fabricated at various cooling rates. Microstructural analyses reveal that RE elements preferentially dissolve into the matrix, while second-phase formation is suppressed at higher cooling rates. RE substitution increases the magnetostriction by enhancing magnetocrystalline distortion energy, while cooling rates act as an effective tuning knob to maximize the <100> texture. Notably, the decreased melting temperature associated with 1 at.% RE doping shifts the optimum texture to lower cooling rate compared with the binary alloy and 0.2 at.% RE doping sample. The magnetostriction as high as 688 ppm is achieved for the 1 at.% Ce doped ribbon fabricated at the speed of 1000 rotation per minute. These results demonstrate that RE-doped melt-spun ribbons are promising candidates for giant magnetostriction and establish a practical processing-texture-property guideline for designing highly magnetostrictive alloys.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates melt-spun Fe81Ga19 ribbons with rare-earth (Pr, Ce) doping and controlled cooling rates to achieve <100> texture and high magnetoelastic anisotropy, reaching 688 ppm magnetostriction in 1 at.% Ce doped ribbons, demonstrating a practical processing-texture-property guideline for designing highly magnetostrictive alloys.
AI.motivation: Single-crystal Fe-Ga is technically demanding and polycrystalline Fe-Ga suffers from low magnetostriction, motivating the exploration of melt-spun ribbons with RE doping and cooling rate optimization as an alternative to achieve controllable <100> texture and required magnetoelastic anisotropy.
AI.method: Fe81Ga19 binary and RE-doped (0.2 at.% Pr, 1 at.% Pr, 1 at.% Ce) ribbons were fabricated via melt-spinning at various cooling rates. Microstructural analyses and magnetostriction measurements were conducted to study the effects of RE doping and cooling rate on texture and magnetoelastic properties.
AI.result: RE elements dissolve into the matrix and suppress second-phase formation at higher cooling rates. RE substitution enhances magnetostriction via increased magnetocrystalline distortion energy; cooling rates tune <100> texture. 1 at.% RE doping lowers melting temperature, shifting optimum texture to lower cooling rate. Maximum magnetostriction of 688 ppm was achieved in 1 at.% Ce doped ribbon at 1000 rpm.
AI.conclusion: RE-doped melt-spun ribbons are promising candidates for giant magnetostriction. The work establishes a practical processing-texture-property guideline for designing highly magnetostrictive alloys.

title: Phase-dependent electronic structure of two-dimensional Ag layers at the graphene/SiC interface
comment: 13 pages, 7 figures, Supplementary information is in the ancillary file
summary: Intercalation at the graphene/SiC interface provides a controlled route to stabilize atomically thin layers with properties distinct from their bulk counterparts. In this platform, the structure and stability of the intercalated phase depend sensitively on the defect landscape of the starting substrate. For intercalated two-dimensional silver at the graphene/SiC interface, two phases have been observed: a phase epitaxial to the SiC lattice, Ag$_{(1)}$, readily obtained following the conventional intercalation method under ultra-high-vacuum conditions and extensively characterized, and a more densely packed phase, called Ag$_{(2)}$, which has remained largely unexplored. Here we report an in situ ultra-high-vacuum preparation method of the second phase intercalated at the graphene/SiC interface; this phase previously was prepared via high-pressure confinement heteroepitaxy. Low-energy electron diffraction shows that Ag$_{(2)}$ is rotated by 30 degree relative to the SiC lattice and forms supercells, in contrast to the $(1\times 1)$ epitaxial relation of Ag$_{(1)}$ with SiC. High-resolution angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy reveals a more rich Ag$_{(2)}$ band dispersion compared to the Ag$_{(1)}$. In density functional theory calculations, by defining the unfolding entropy which, in a quantified way, finds that the band structure of Ag$_{(2)}$ is more suitable to be unfolded to the SiC primitive cell, and the resulting unfolded band dispersion is in great agreement with the experimental data. We further show that the different intercalated Ag phases tune the electronic properties of the overlying quasi-free-standing graphene layer differently: compared with Ag$_{(1)}$, Ag$_{(2)}$ yields an $\sim$1.75 times higher charge carrier density and modifies the charge-plasmon interaction of the graphene layer, indicating a change in effective screening at the interface.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an in situ ultra-high-vacuum method to prepare a densely packed Ag₂ phase intercalated at the graphene/SiC interface (previously only achievable via high-pressure confinement heteroepitaxy), characterizes its distinct structural and electronic properties compared to the known Ag₁ phase, and demonstrates that Ag₂ induces higher charge carrier density and modified plasmon interactions in the overlying graphene layer.
AI.motivation: The second intercalated silver phase (Ag₂) at the graphene/SiC interface had remained largely unexplored due to the lack of a controllable preparation method under ultra-high-vacuum conditions; the authors aim to develop such a method and characterize its structure and electronic properties.
AI.method: In situ ultra-high-vacuum preparation of Ag₂ intercalated at graphene/SiC; structural characterization using low-energy electron diffraction (LEED); electronic structure investigation via high-resolution angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES); theoretical analysis using density functional theory (DFT) with a novel "unfolding entropy" metric; comparison of graphene's charge carrier density and plasmon interactions between Ag₁ and Ag₂ phases.
AI.result: Ag₂ is rotated by 30° relative to the SiC lattice and forms supercells (vs. 1×1 epitaxy for Ag₁); ARPES reveals richer band dispersion for Ag₂; DFT with unfolding entropy confirms the band structure is better unfolded to the SiC primitive cell; Ag₂ yields ~1.75× higher charge carrier density in graphene and modifies the charge-plasmon interaction compared to Ag₁.
AI.conclusion: The in situ UHV method successfully yields the Ag₂ phase, and the different intercalated Ag phases provide tunable control over the electronic properties (carrier density, screening, plasmon interactions) of the quasi-free-standing graphene layer.

title: Photoluminescent Tetragonal Tb-doped Pb2P2O7
summary: In this study, we report the synthesis and characterization of a novel tetragonal polymorph of Tb-doped Pb2P2O7. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction confirms the stabilization of the P41 and P43 enantiomorphs at room temperature due to the incorporation of Tb3+ ions. Optical investigations reveal green photoluminescence from the characteristic 5D4 -> 7Fj (J = 1-5) transitions of Tb3+, with each emission split due to the crystal field effect, indicating the presence of Tb3+ in multiple coordination environments. The power dependence of the PL intensity follows a linear power-law behavior, suggesting a one-photon excitation process. Temperature-dependent PL measurements show an initial increase in intensity up to 125C, attributed to energy transfer from structural defects, followed by thermal quenching above this temperature. Structural stability at elevated temperatures is confirmed via high-temperature X-ray diffraction (XRD), showing no phase transitions before melting at approximately 800C. These findings highlight the potential of tetragonal Tb-doped Pb2P2O7 as a new class of photoluminescent material.

AI.tldr: This paper reports the synthesis, structural characterization, and photoluminescent properties of a new tetragonal polymorph of Tb-doped Pb2P2O7, which exhibits green photoluminescence from Tb3+ transitions, linear power-law excitation behavior, and thermal stability up to ~800°C.
AI.motivation: To develop a new class of photoluminescent materials by stabilizing a novel tetragonal polymorph of Pb2P2O7 through Tb3+ doping, and to understand its structural and optical properties.
AI.method: Synthesis of Tb-doped Pb2P2O7; characterization via single-crystal X-ray diffraction (to confirm P41/P43 enantiomorphs), photoluminescence (PL) spectroscopy (power dependence and temperature-dependent measurements from 25°C to 125°C+), and high-temperature XRD to assess structural stability up to ~800°C.
AI.result: Green photoluminescence from Tb3+ 5D4→7Fj transitions with crystal-field splitting; linear power dependence (one-photon excitation); PL intensity increases up to 125°C due to defect-mediated energy transfer, then thermal quenching; no structural phase transitions before melting at ~800°C.
AI.conclusion: Tetragonal Tb-doped Pb2P2O7 is a promising new photoluminescent material with good thermal stability and interesting temperature-dependent emission behavior, suitable for potential optical applications.
